turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, this computer's crawled to a halt again. You're Mr Hartley, the diabetes review, yes? Bear with me while the notes decide to load.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Graham, yeah. We were circling the car park twenty minutes, some van dumped across two bays, and I nearly just went home. Anyway, we're here.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm Linda, his wife. I booked him in. His sugars have been all over the shop and he just shrugs.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Nurse, what's on the medication list while I find the right tab? I've clicked into someone else's letters.
[SEG0005] person_4 (NURSE): Repeat script is metformin one gram twice a day, and insulin glargine, Lantus, 28 units at night.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): No, that's not right. I do, um, 24... no, 22. They cut it after I went hypo at my sister's barbecue, last autumn. 28 was the old dose.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again, I was in the wrong box. Was it 22?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): 22. I dial 22 on the pen. Well, most nights I do.
[SEG0009] person_4 (NURSE): The chart still says 28 units once nightly, doctor. If someone changed it, they never updated this.
[SEG0010] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He tells me 22, and I've watched him dial it a few times. I'm not there every single evening, mind.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which nights are you not taking it, then?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Early shifts. I'm on the forklift at the depot from six, so on a work day I skip the injection. Don't want a hypo halfway up a rack. Weekends I'm good, I take it.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the metformin, you're actually swallowing that?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, a thousand milligrams in the morning and again with my tea. Don't miss those, they're just tablets. Been on them years.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): My mate Dave's on some weekly jab and he will not shut up about it. We were meant to go fishing Sunday, only the rain was filthy, so that was that.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. What were those home sugars? Someone's scribbled a figure and I can't read my own writing.

[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Fasting it's, um, one-eighty-something. Well, actually I looked this morning and I can't remember if it was 186 or 181. I don't write them down, the book's under the batteries and the dog lead.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): One-eighty? Say that again, is your meter still in the old American numbers?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): It comes up 180, or 186, something round there, before breakfast. I never changed the setting. After meals I don't bother, life's too short.
[SEG0020] person_4 (NURSE): Finger-prick in the room this morning was 11.4. Blood pressure 146 over 88, pulse 78, weight 91.5 kilos.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ta. Any thirst, or getting up at night to wee?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Thirsty, yeah, I'm on the squash all day. And I'm up once or twice in the night, which is new these last few months. Knackered with it, if I'm honest.
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's shattered. Asleep in the chair before the news most nights.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Feet. Any numbness, tingling, sores between the toes?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No, feet are fine. I walk the dog every evening, no tingling, nothing like sores. Had a verruca years back, gone now.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the eyes? Any blurring, or have you had the screening photos?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Eyes are all right. Photos last spring, letter said all clear. I squint at the telly but that's wanting new glasses, I've been on about that since Christmas.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll have a look while this thing restarts. Skin on both feet is intact, no breaks, the pulses are there, and the monofilament sensation is normal.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, penicillin or otherwise?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing. Penicillin's fine, never had a rash or anything.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long's the diabetes been? Remind me, the summary box is blank.

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Diagnosed about eight years back. My dad had it too, type two, he was on insulin near the end. Mum's side, nothing of the sort. Linda still buys the chocolate digestives, mind, I have the one with my tea.

[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to conclude the dose is wrong. It might be the injections you skip on shift days, or 22 units might simply not be enough, and I can't separate those two from here. The home numbers are too woolly to hang a decision on.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): So I'll send you for an HbA1c today, before anyone changes the insulin. Nurse can do the blood on your way out.
[SEG0035] person_4 (NURSE): Chair's free, I can take it before half ten. Just the HbA1c, yeah?

[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. And Graham, don't just skip the injection on work mornings. If the forklift and hypos are the worry, we can shift the timing, but missing it is muddying this. Write the fasting figures down for a fortnight, actual numbers.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in six weeks and we'll go through the result. Reception will book it, assuming this computer's alive.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks is fine, long as it's not an early. I'm on earlies all next month. Cheers, then.

spec.situation: Type 2 diabetic on tablets plus insulin; patient and nurse give different insulin doses, patient skips doses on work days, reads home sugar numbers aloud in a muddled way ('one-eighty-something fasting'). Foot and eye questions.
features: disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

bad.reason: Nurse reports once nightly insulin glargine, but dose omitted and patient disputes consistent current use.

omissions.text: Insulin glargine current patient-reported dose is 22 units on the pen, with 28 units nightly being the old dose reduced after a hypoglycaemic episode last autumn; the recorded medication entry lists insulin glargine once nightly from the nurse list but omits/could misstate the patient-reported 22-unit dose.
Insulin glargine is not taken every night: the patient skips it on early-shift work days and says he takes it on weekends; recording it simply as once nightly is misleading.
Home fasting glucose readings are very high at about 180-186 on a meter still set to old American numbers, before breakfast; this was discussed as the relevant home sugar pattern.
The patient does not check post-meal glucose readings ('After meals I don't bother').
Blurred vision was specifically asked about and denied ('Eyes are all right'); only squinting at the television/new glasses was recorded.
Diabetic eye screening photos were last spring and the letter said they were all clear.
Penicillin was specifically asked about and denied as an allergy ('Penicillin's fine, never had a rash or anything').
Family history also included that the mother's side had no diabetes ('Mum's side, nothing of the sort').
